utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Savkic, I was asking you some questions in relation to an act of sabotage that you were describing to the Court. As a result, you said of -- from the information we saw in tab 6 -- could we go to tab 6, please. The question I need to ask you is the acts of sabotage that you described, and I could read them out to you again if need be -- well, first of all, did they actually ever take place? Were these various -- the tunnel you've described and the road, were they ever blown-up, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gentlemen, yes. The bridge in Nova Kasaba, there was an attempt at blowing it up. It was not completely destroyed; however, as of that moment on, it could no longer be used because most of the bridge collapsed. When I spoke about the sabotage at the tunnel on the road towards the mine, I can also say that most of the tunnel collapsed, and in front of it there was a timber barricade some several tens of metres long. So that road was also impassable. And the third incident --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. On what basis do you link those two incidents, they'll do fine for this purpose, with this or any other document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a generally known fact that while preparations were being made for armament and preparation of explosives, that the quantity of explosives that had been seized at the time, and it was obvious that this person in addition to crimes related to armament with automatic weapons, did the same with the explosives. The explosives cannot be used for anything else in such a situation but to destroy things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, time-frame for these acts of sabotage, could you please elicit that from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could tell us the dates of each -- of the three instances. I stopped you from telling the Court about the third because I wanted to establish the basis, first of all. When did each one of the incidents occur, please?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These instances took place before the front line was established between the Serb and the Muslim forces. To be more precise, during the period between the month of April and 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I want to, in fact, go back and return briefly to a topic you were giving evidence about yesterday, simply because I failed to deal with a particular document and then I will return to the subject of arming that you begun telling the Chamber about. Tab 16, please. Mr. Savkic, we can see, can't we, that this is some sort of MUP document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you obtain this particular document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obtained this document through a friend of mine. He was still at the time the chief of the public security station in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what is significant about this document, please?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance of this document lies in the facts that I spoke about yesterday, namely, the Muslim side had sent its policemen, i.e., candidates selected by the SDA, for training in Croatia, although this should have been done in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The biggest centre for the training of the police was in Sremska Kamenica in Vojvodina, that is in Serbia, so they could have been sent there as well. It transpires from this document that the assistant minister of the interior, Mirsad Srebrenikovic did that, and only a month or so before that he had been appointed assistant minister as an SDA nominee. This is about the document where 1685 is indicated, if you are referring to this document. I must say that at that time in Croatia, there had already been a state in place. They obtained their own state in February 1992. They had seceded from Yugoslavia. So there could not have been any good intentions behind sending the police for training in a state that had broken up from the federal state, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was still a republic in that federal state. This is indisputable. Yesterday I spoke about the reasons why these policemen were sent to there. The purpose, intent, of that training was to hide something that the Serbian part of the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina should not have been privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll stop you. We dealt with that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, tab 16 needs a number, I take it. Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D133, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Judge Hanoteau has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I see something rather ambiguous in what you've just said. Could you clarify what you've said. These people who were sent to Croatia, were they professional policemen who were sent, seconded to Croatia, or were they people who were going to Croatia for training before becoming -- or before passing an exam or some sort of competitive exam before becoming a policeman, an official policeman. Could you clarify this point, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After a medical check-up, these men were sent to Croatia. Many of them did not have any previous education. They were sent there for a course, after which they were admitted into the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What is obvious here is the fact that - and I emphasise once again something that can be seen on tab 6 - that only those people were sent there that were nominated by the SDA from certain municipalities. And you can see clearly under tab 6 how those people were chosen. I don't know whether any of them had previous training or secondary education. I cannot either deny or contest that or confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we just briefly deal with the list. The documents, for the purpose of translation, have been split up. But as you understand it, the list of 448 names was effectively attached to the letter from Mr. Srebrenikovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, do you know the ethnicity of Mr. Srebrenikovic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although ethnic affiliation is a personal thing; however, judging by the name and the way he was selected by the SDA, there is no doubt that he is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have conducted a cursory look at this list of 448 names, and based on your knowledge of name -- of Bosnian names, what are you able to tell us about the ethnic breakdown of these 448 names, please?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I look at these people who had met the requirements of this medical check-up, it s obvious that the requirements were met mostly by Muslims and Croats, by and large. One can conclude that not only by their names but also when it comes to the Croats, the Croat and Serb names are rather similar. However, one can draw that conclusion from the names of the municipalities where they came from. It is a notorious fact that some of the municipalities are predominantly Muslim or Serb or Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, Mr. Savkic, because I wasn't asking you for the basis of your methodology. But what was the result of your are research through these 448 names? I think you -- you've marked it, haven't you, on the very last page, very last page of the bundle?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the last page, it is to do the maths and see that out of 313 candidates that met the requirements, 135 were non-Muslims -- actually, those were all Croats. The rest were all Muslims. However, I have to clarify one more thing and to go back and do a reality check. During that period - and not only during that period of time - to send Serbs to Zagreb for training, given the well-known developments would have been crazy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I understand, but please correct me if I'm wrong, I understand the methodology of which you said you are not that much interested in to be the following: That if by name you could identify someone as a Muslim then, of course, you would accept that he's a Muslim; that there were 135 non-Muslims; and since Croats and Serbs could not be distinguished through their names, that on the basis of predominantly -- of the predominant population of a municipality, that one could establish that the non-Muslims were Croats. You said you're not interested in the methodology. It seems to be very relevant if you want to draw conclusions, and especially to say that if a name could not be identified as a Muslim name, then by the predominance of the population, I would conclude that it must be a Croat -- and also for reasons of logic because you would not send a Serb to Croatia for training, that is -- well, that methodology needs to be further explained in order to accept the conclusions drawn on the basis of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't and wouldn't possibly argue with that. If the Chamber are interested in the methodology, then it's something I'll explore with the witness. I can only apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if it is what he told us until now, that's a mixture of logic and conclusions -- I mean, if 10 per cent of a population is Serb and 10 per cent Muslim and 80 per cent is Croat, and if the name doesn't identify anyone, then of course, on the basis of the municipality being predominantly Croat is -- but -- let's say, I leave it up to you whether you want to further explore it. I just wanted to let you know that until now the methodology is not a very convincing basis for drawing conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, you've said, haven't you, that apart from anything else you think it's extremely unlikely that any Serb would actually go on such a training course. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, for well-known reasons. However, it is a historical fact that not a single Serb went on that training. This is a notorious fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we move back to the issue of arming, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are at least two documents which I would now like to turn to, which are the subject of challenges by the Prosecution. I've discussed the matter briefly with both my learned friends. We're of the view, subject to -- the Chamber has to say that really the witness should probably be asked to leave court because they do require a ruling from Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Savkic, we have to deal with a procedural issue which should be discussed in your absence. Therefore, I'd like to is you to follow Madam Usher for a second. We'll hear the parties on the matter, and then we'll invite you to return. It has got nothing to do with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wasn't it 2 and 8, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What would be the best way, Mr. Josse? Would you introduce the matter and then that we hear the objection by Mr. Margetts, or would you say that Mr. Margetts could immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I'll briefly introduce the matter, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to turn to tab 2 next. I was going to invite the witness to produce the statement that we see there. I was going to invite him to explain how it came into his possession. I don't think, in reality, there's any dispute as to its authenticity by the Prosecution, though I stand to be corrected in due course by Your Honour about that. And in my submission, once the witness can, one, explain how it came into his possession; and two, give some useful, further information in relation to it -- be in a position to comment on it, it's admissible as a document produced in time in the normal course of events. Might I make this observation in passing: It can't be any less admissible than the frequent newspaper articles that were put to the witnesses in this case, but I can develop that in due course if I need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for our understanding -- of course we'll have to ask the witness. But who you would -- who gave this statement to whom as far as you can read it? And what's exactly on the basis of the text the relevance of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This was a statement that the author made to the MUP in Vlasenica. It amounts to a confession to smuggling of arms. It obviously followed his arrest by them. The relevance is: It indicates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the same person as we earlier had --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: These are all different people, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A similar smuggler, perhaps, or arms trader, but not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a statement containing a confession made to the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, we communicated to Mr. Josse a couple of days ago that we would take objection to both tabs 2 and tabs 8 which are statements given to the Vlasenica public security station after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We come to 8 later, I take it? Only 2 has been introduced until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, dealing with tab 2, that's a statement that's given to the Vlasenica public security station on the 23rd of April, 1992. And Your Honours have heard that Vlasenica was taken over on the 20th of April. Subsequent to that people were taken to the Vlasenica public security station and interrogated. The objection was based on three rules. In our view, a statement of this nature should be either introduced through the 92 bis methodology when the witness is not present, if the witness -- if the deponent of this statement can be present, and possibly 89(F) would be a basis for producing this statement. The third ground we objected to this statement under was Rule 95, effectively that we say that this statement was obtained by means which cast substantial doubt on its reliability. The first point, though, addressing Mr. Josse's specific submission that this statement has no different character than a newspaper article, we flatly reject that submission. A newspaper article has various purposes of evidential value. One of the purposes is the substantive nature of the information contained in a newspaper article; the other purpose is, in fact, the fact that the information was communicated to the public in general and it goes to other issues in this case such as knowledge. So this statement cannot be compared with newspaper articles, and, quite rightly, newspaper articles are treated in a completely different manner and have been throughout this trial than statements. Whenever the Prosecution has sought to introduce statements of this nature, it has been through the 89(F) or 92 bis method. The exceptions to that are only when a particular witness has given evidence of the intent or disposition or circumstances of an individual who has given a statement, and we have challenged that version of events by reference to a statement given by that individual. Before I proceed any further, I should inform the Trial Chamber that the deponent of this statement which is the document at tab 2, Munib Ahmetovic gave a statement to the Tribunal in January 1995, where he set out the circumstances preceding the giving of his statements and the circumstances in which he gave this statement. I have copies of that statement, which I would like to hand up to the Tribunal -- to the Chamber. And I have provided -- I provided a copy of that statement to the Defence yesterday. Effectively what he says is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to stop my learned friend for a moment and ask the Chamber to distill these issues because why, I submit, does my learned friend say that the provision of this statement to this Court now assists this Court in determining the issue of admissibility of the document that the Defence are putting before you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it -- I did understand, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that Mr. Margetts was intending to present to us a document which would, I would say, basically support the reliance on Rule 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, then could I, just before that's done, respond to the submission of the two. It may be that Mr. Margetts will still say: Notwithstanding the way I put it, the Court needs to see this statement and I won't object further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will give you an opportunity, then, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- submission is -- my response to what my learned friend has said hitherto is that the submission is totally misconceived, with respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just stop here. Is it the fact that Mr. Josse intends to restrict his response to 89(F) and 92 bis or does intend of us Rule 95? Because in our submission -- I haven't completed my submissions in regard to Rule 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may complete your submissions, that's not a problem, but I think you wanted to present to the Court that document and what I understand Mr. Josse said: Before you do so I would like to respond to what has been said until now and which could influence our decision on whether or not we would allow you to present this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. If my learned friend doesn't accept what I'm saying now, I won't argue further and the document can go before the Court, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- I would object to Mr. Josse responding to any of my submissions and I would say that he should only be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Margetts takes that response, then I'll let him present the statement to the Court. If he wants to be pedantic like that, I'm not going to argue with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't -- I request that that remark be struck from the record. This is not pedantic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not withdrawing any remarks --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- before this Court to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although I haven't -- I claim a relevant knowledge of the English language, I have to look up what the word means. So as far as -- at this moment matters stand, although it's on the record, I could not decide whether it should stay on the record because in -- and I'm not asking for any explanation at this very moment, but sometimes there are words I am not familiar with. I should have listened perhaps to the Defence translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In Deutsch, es ist "pedantische."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said I didn't ask for an explanation, but Mr. Margetts seems to misunderstand my English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Being that we're gentlemen common lawyers, we're both now sitting down. I said I'm not going to deal with this in this way. If Mr. Margetts wants to hand the statement to the Court, then perhaps that's the best thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I would have given you an opportunity, but if you refrain from it -- Mr. Margetts, you may proceed, and you're invited to use words I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I will hand the statement up. I have copies here, four copies. Your Honours, I think probably the most expeditious way to proceed is for Your Honours to read the entire statement because it only covers the period of three days and all of the matters in it do set the scene for the specific issue at stake -- the issue that arises in 95 that expressly at the bottom of page 5 and the top of page 6, there is an express denial of all of the matters that appear in tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course I have no objection to that, but I do hope that the Chamber will, first of all, read the statement in tab 2, because otherwise it's absurd. It literally is putting the cart before the horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- one of my problems at tab 2 at this moment is -- because one of the first questions that came into my mind when the issue was raised was: When was this person arrested? Because you said it apparently is a statement given after his arrest. And in view of the date of the take-over, of course, one of the first things I was thinking about was whether the arrest was made before or after the take-over. The statement is not completely translated, and, for example, this information which I was seeking I could not at first sight -- find. So therefore, at least where this seems to be a sensitive issue, the only partial translation is a handicap.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's -- that very thought crossed my mind and -- yes, that's the position that the Chamber finds itself in, I regret to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before the Chamber rules on the objection - and keeping in mind that this witness has several times referred to what was general knowledge and what was logic and what was a notorious fact, he may have known that notorious facts need not to be proven at all, so there's even no need to speak about notorious facts - but what could the witness tell us on the basis of the document you wanted to confront him with?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it's best to ask him that directly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then he's confronted with it and -- has he been present when this statement was taken, at least did you assume that he was present?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I do not think he was present. I do not understand that he was present further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You could say, because it was the witness who will tell us. If he was not present, what type of questions would you like to put to him in relation to this document? And if you tendered the document it could have -- it could be interpreted in different ways. Would you oppose to the other statement to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would. I would, and I can develop my argument if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- if I need to and if the Court would allow me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because one of the problems would be that this statement could be either evidence which would support that the person involved was trading arms and distributing arms to Muslims, but it could also be evidence of statements forced by the police at that time, false statements forcibly given to the police. So the probative value of this document could be very much in favour of the Defence case and, at the same time, could also be very much in favour of the Prosecution case. But, of course, we would not know what he would say, and therefore I wonder how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, that's a problem for the trier of facts in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Namely, you and your brother Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's an issue that the parties, if they choose, can address at the appropriate time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- at the end of this case. I have made a robust decision that I want this document in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear, and the Prosecution objects. And the Chamber is confronted with a Rule 95 objection and the Chamber should explore that objection to see -- and at the same time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not suggesting otherwise, let me hastily add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what one usually does if such an objection is raised, to ask the Prosecution: What makes you believe that this would be a statement which would not be admissible under Rule 95? And we would invite them to produce whatever they have in order to decide that matter. That's what they're doing now more or less --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you object against this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- and this was the point that I was going to make a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A point that Mr. Margetts understandably insisted that the Chamber read the Prosecution's statement. The point I was going to make is: His submission, I contend, is fundamentally misconceived. It's fundamentally misconceived because the Defence are not seeking to put this document in under Rule 92 bis or 89(F). So far is Rule 95 is concerned, well, I submit that only applies to a statement that would be tendered either under 92 bis or under 89(F). The point here -- this is a document produced in 1992 at the time of war that this case is trying at the moment and is effectively an original document. The weight that you and your colleagues, Your Honour, attach to this document is another matter altogether. But it's completely different to the statement the Prosecution have provided, which is a statement that has been compiled in contemplation of proceedings. I'm not going to say these proceedings, but in contemplation of proceeding. And therefore, clearly, would only be admissible, for example, under 89 (F) or 92 bis. Could I draw an analogy? I think it's P780, lost my note for a moment, that was series of statements that were deduced in evidence by Mr. Davidovic of members of the Yellow Wasps whom he, Davidovic, had taken into custody. The best argument I suspect the Prosecution could come up with in distinguishing P780 which is about 30-odd statements, and this particular document is that Davidovic had some personal part in the taking of those statements. But frankly, from recollection, it was quite a long time ago, he physically wasn't involved in taking all 30-odd statements. That wasn't possible. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So I would draw an analogy between those kind of statements and this statement. It's effectively an original document, if I can put it like that. The weight to be attached to it is a different matter altogether. Your Honour, if the Prosecution were going to say: We readily accept that each and every hearsay document they have presented this Court, save those under 92 bis and 89(F) have not been deduced as to the truth of their contents, then I assume the Defence would jump for joy and say: That's marvelous. The thousands -- I'm exaggerating slightly, but the hundreds of documents, for example, newspaper articles that have been deduced in this case, we don't have to worry about them. As for the truth of the contents, they're only there for some sort of contextual-type purpose. From -- that would make everyone's life very much easier. But that isn't the case, I suspect. As I say, I don't think I need to develop my argument much further. The basic submission advanced by the Prosecution is rather, I submit, missing the point about this statement. And the witness will put it into context as best he can. The Court may take the view there is insufficient nexus between the witness and the statement. That's a different matter and, really, the Court can't rule upon that until they've heard from the witness and as to his connection with the statement and his knowledge of its contents. That's how I put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Margetts, Mr. Josse has responded to your objection. Is there any need to -- for further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could, I would make some very brief comments. The first is that the solution proposed or suggested is a possibility by Your Honour is one that we would not oppose, and that is that both the statement at tab 2 and the further statement be introduced. In our submission, the further statement is one that the Court may more readily be prepared to admit into evidence for the fact that it's quite clearly not taken in circumstances where there was coercion. The next point I would make is this: Mr. Josse's comments are creative, would be our submission, but we never understood that Rule 95 only applied to 89(F) or 92 bis statements; that's certainly something that's new to me -- or not new to me, but it's something that we reject. The next thing is the analogy with P780 is, to use Mr. Josse's expression, fundamentally misconceived. Your Honours will recall the purpose or the issues that those statements went to when they were introduced through Mr. Davidovic and with the protected witness. There is a certain element of the fact that the 7(3) case was in issue at the time, also notice as to crimes that have been committed, also the capacity of the security forces to detain those who they wished for purposes they -- purposes that they deemed appropriate. The matters that were not addressed in the statement -- in those statements were the substance -- were in part the substance of why we asked for P780 to be introduced. It's an entirely different matter to this -- the introduction of this statement. This is a very simple attempt by the Defence to subvert the Rules in regard to the introduction of statements that support substantive parts of their positive case. The Rules are clear. It's 92 bis or it's 89(F); they were applied stringently with the Prosecution. We have not introduced statements of this nature for the purpose for which the Defence wishes to introduce this statement. So in our submission, either tab 2 should be excluded or, alternatively, the solution of both of these statements being introduced that was crafted by Your Honour. It may be an appropriate way forward thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, would you please respond and would you include in your response the observations made by Mr. Margetts as to the applicability of Rule 95 only to 92 bis statements or 89(F) statements, especially in view of the fact that Rule 95 existed for quite some time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- before Rule 92 bis was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue that point, and I've said what's said, save for this, of course. Again, it's the cart before the horse. The Court is going to have to decide the extent to which they use the Prosecution's statement, whether it's admitted in evidence or not, in order to exclude the Defence -- the exhibit that we're trying to put before the Court. I say that because, of course, it doesn't automatically follow that what's contained within that statement is true. We've had no opportunity to cross-examine the deponent, just like, of course, the Prosecution haven't had any opportunity to cross-examine the deponent in the sense of what he's saying in the statement that we are producing. I accept that. Could I make two comments? First of all, I rely rather heavily on Mr. Margetts' use of the word "in part" when he refers to P780. It may well be right that in part it was put in evidence in reliance of what he's just said, but it's the rest of it that may concern the Chamber. Secondly, I would draw this analogy, Your Honour, supposing, supposing Mr. Davidovic had been cross-examined - dare I go into this subject again - with a statement that was purportedly written by one of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was purportedly written by one of the members of the Yellow Wasps and had been obtained by the Defence, and it said: You, Mr. Davidovic, you and your men forced this statement out of me and that's why I made it. The Prosecution would have jumped up and said: We've got no evidence of the provenance of this statement which the Defence are producing. And if the Defence had suggested: Well, okay, P780 is going to go in but the now reverse, the statement produced by the Defence also needs to go in, the Court wouldn't have contemplated that particular course. The fact that the statement that you have been provided with has been taken by OTP investigators rather than, for example, Defence investigators, the fact that it appears, rather grandly, on ICTY note-paper doesn't mean to say it's anymore admissible than a document the Defence would have produced in exactly the same circumstances which would have been laughed out of court. So I mention that in terms of equality of approach that the Chamber might want to bear in mind when they come to contemplate this particular matter in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will take an early break to consider the matter, and upon return we'll give our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, one other comment, thinking aloud, may I address the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we should deal with 8 as well, because otherwise we would have to take another early break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. And what I was going to suggest, with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- is that, and perhaps I should have done it this originally but the witness being back -- to come back into court and deal with both documents purely - and I will lead him as best I can in relation to this - as to how they came into his possession. In particular 8 is a more problematical document because it's handwritten. He has the original of 8 with him, as a matter of fact, and gives the Chamber some idea as to the extent to which he's able to comment on the matters contained within it. I -- that's what I'd invite the Court to do at this particular juncture. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We always need to be realistic about it. The Chamber's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first -- we do look at these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So perhaps there is -- at least there is some -- AP 8 stands, as far as you understand, Mr. Josse, for -- you must have an idea on -- I see bazooka is a word I know. Winchester I can relate to a rifle. Singapore is a capital in Asia for me. PAP and AP, apart from "associated press," I take it that it's a reference to weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Firearms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Firearms, yes. AP stands just for firearms?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Automatic pistol -- rifle, sorry. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Automatic rifle, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Singapore stands for?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. But it seems all references to -- we'll then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Effectively, Your Honour, could I put it like this? And perhaps I should have done this earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm inviting the court to have a voir dire as to what the witness knows about the document, because I submit that's bound to help in determining whether -- their admissibility. That's not always the case, but here, I submit, it's bound to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not before we have heard the objection by Mr. Margetts, because then we know better what we are talking about. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this statement on its face has very little to support an argument that it should be something admitted and relied upon by this Trial Chamber. It seems to be note -- notes that, without any further information, we assume were written in the same circumstances as the statement of Mr. Ahmetovic. That would be notes written during the course of an interrogation. And the date seems to indicate that probably around about the same time as the interrogation of Mr. Ahmetovic. Now, Mr. Ahmetovic has explained, very well, the circumstances in Vlasenica at the time that these interrogations were conducted. Other witnesses before this Trial Chamber have also described the circumstances in Vlasenica at the time that these notes were compiled. And on the basis of that, we would say that those circumstances described would suggest that this statement was given in the statement circumstances as the statement given by Mr. Ahmetovic. Furthermore, the actual content of this statement is such that it -- it seems to be more akin to a propaganda bulletin of the Serbs than as to an honest statement from a Muslim. The expressions "Green Berets" are used. There's a reference to a Muslim going around wearing the chest-board symbol associated with Croats. Later on we've got the reference to "green uniforms" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is comment on the content and the -- whether it is -- I mean, who used the expression "Green Berets" we do not know. Whether or not it's right that someone was going around wearing chest-board. If you say this is propaganda, it could be facts as well, Mr. Margetts, so there's no need to speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm attempting to put to Your Honour the fact of these inconsistencies in the statement itself indicate that it is a statement that has been coerced from the deponent. And I only had one further reference and that is that a chap by the name of Damir Hadzic has a "U" tattooed on his left side which is the symbol of the Ustasha. Again, that's a fairly unlikely scenario --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this is really all speculation, Mr. Margetts. Whether it's likely or not is -- I do understand you say the statement is taken at approximately the same time in the circumstances the Prosecution considers such that this document should have the same fate as number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I too say just in my defence and in the defence of my submission, that the Court has heard substantial evidence as to the type of propaganda statements that were made by the Serbs and the types of things that when non-Serbs were detained they were forced to say and forced to admit. And I'm only drawing the Court's attention to the fact that this statement is consistent with that evidence that the Trial Chamber has heard. And so I would that's the second link of my submission, that it can be inferred from the evidence that the Trial Chamber has heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't it true, Mr. Margetts, that especially the presentation of the Defence case is there to challenge, to undermine, to dispute whatever evidence has been heard in the Prosecution's case. So to say: We were first, we have presented evidence which -- which demonstrates that these are false statements, you could say exactly the other way around to say: See, here we have statements given at the time, statements that demonstrate that all of the evidence that says that Serbs were arming, that Serbs were forcing Muslims, is totally untrue and that is demonstrated by this material we are presenting now. Therefore, we could not, on the basis of the Prosecution case, determine the matter. Mr. Josse, any need to further respond to Mr. Margetts' observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will follow the suggestion made by Mr. Josse. That means that before we decide whether or not tabs 2 and 8 will be admitted into evidence and before we decide whether or not the statement presented by the Prosecution will be admitted into evidence, that we'll hear from the witness a bit more about provenance of these documents and also what he knows about it, what he could tell us about it. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Savkic into the courtroom. I'm afraid, Mr. Josse, that the early break will be the normal break. The handicap of the incompleteness of tab 2 is still there, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we'd endorse that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I even might put already a few questions first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm more than happy, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, could you please have a look at a document which appears under tab 2. Let's just -- I do understand that you may have an original or something like that, but let's just at this moment keep it to what we have here. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He's getting his spectacles, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, his spectacles. No, Mr. Josse explains to me that you wanted to take your spectacles out of your bag, which of course is allowed. Have you seen this document before, a document which seems to be a statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I saw this document at the time when it was drafted, on the 23rd of April, 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to put very precise questions, and I want you to answer those questions and those questions only. So my question was: Have you seen this document before? I take it then that the answer is: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what day did you for the first time see this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either on the 23rd or the 24th of April. In any case, I saw it when it was the most topical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who gave it to you at that time, when you saw it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of the public security station in Vlasenica showed it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you present when the statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any further knowledge about the circumstances under which this statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even before this date, the chief informed us about Imam Ahmetovic case. Even before this date we had information according to which he was amongst those that were engaged in the activities described in this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any document which dates from -- well, let's say before the -- before the 20th of April, 1992, which contains information about what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to the contents of this information, I can say that I don't remember having seen any other statement, a signed statement, to that effect. If you're referring to the process of armament, then I can say that I did see information about people being armed. For example, the Muslim villages in Kladanj municipality, and then my answer would be: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if you have any knowledge you could be asked about that by Mr. Josse, but that's not directly in relation to this document from what I understand. What could you add from your personal knowledge to this document on the events described in it which we could not read from this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, I'd like to say that I know that this unfortunate man, after this statement, had certain problems posed by Muslims and Serbs alike. And I know that our priest, together with the priest from Vlasenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again because I asked you what you could add from your personal knowledge to the events that are described in this statement, not what happened to this person afterwards, not what -- but just on the events that are described here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that many people that he mentions here in this statement will be mentioned by others as well. In other words, what was already known will appear in other people's statements, and these people will be mentioned as those who had continuously been involved in the armament of Muslims in those municipalities what I have mentioned. I'm referring to the Kavazbasic brothers, I've already mentioned one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. May I -- I do understand that you say: What I could add to it is that I know that statements pointing at the same persons are taken and that comparison would teach that one document would support the other. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I invite the court to go into either closed or private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will do so. Mr. Josse, as I said, I wanted to put a few questions first. I will give you an opportunity at a later stage to add any questions you would like, but we will now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before I give the ruling of the Chamber, could you please assist us. We tried to check but P780 was not objected to, was it? It was a contextual document, report, accompanied by a lot of statements, to which reference was made in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do not think it was objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't checked it specifically. I was here at the time. I wasn't conducting the case at that particular juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that the P780 was introduced through Ms. Edgerton and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, she was at least there when the Chamber said that objections could be raised within one week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton at that moment was there. And I could not find anywhere objections made against 780.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm certainly prepared to concede and accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, how far that takes the Court is a matter for Your Honour. The use of the word "contextual," might I mention in passing is perhaps significant. Use of Your Honour's word "contextual," in regard to the submissions the Court's heard from both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll give the ruling. The Chamber has considered that this witness apparently has nothing to -- nothing which would have such a relevance that it would lead us to another decision, has nothing to add to the two statements as such. Given the -- and in view of the objections made, the Chamber also considers that the witness has no first-hand knowledge. And I know that first-hand knowledge is not always required, but under the specific circumstances and in view of the objection, that the Chamber considers that the witness has no first-hand knowledge on the circumstances under which the statement was taken. The Chamber therefore considers that this witness should not be the vehicle through which these statements would be introduced into evidence. If the Defence would like to introduce the statements into evidence, then Rule 92 bis might be the appropriate route to take and the Chamber then expects that the Prosecution -- and the Chamber already says that it would grant such a request, that the Prosecution would insist, at least, on cross-examination of the witness who gave that statement. And then of course the full 95 -- Rule 95 objection would then have to be thoroughly explored before a decision on admission could be made. The Chamber also considers that Rule 95 doesn't leave much room for the Chamber to say: We'll evaluate at a later stage or we'll see what the value is, because Rule 95 clearly indicates that evidence is not admissible if it's obtained under certain circumstances. So the Chamber considers that it has not much margin of appreciation there. Therefore, Mr. Josse, you'll not be allowed to introduce through this witness the tabs 2 and 8, and the Chamber will also -- I -- the Chamber has understood the statement presented by the Prosecution as tendered only in case tabs 2 and 8 would be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the only matter that remains is to what extent tabs 2 and 8 and the document presented by the Defence should be made available if ever an appeal would be lodged against the judgement of this Chamber, and therefore one of the solutions would be to mark them for identification, but then all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm neutral about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that that leaves to the Appeals Chamber. If there would be any complaint on appeal that the Chamber took a wrong decision in this respect, that at least the Appeals Chamber would know what the documents were we are talking about. Therefore, Mr. Registrar, could you please give numbers, MFI numbers, for, first, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 2, Your Honours, would be D134 MFI. Tab 8 would be D135 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I add the D and the P numbers for MFI or? I'll talk about the numbering with -- with the representative of the registry. For the time being we have these numbers, and then the statement presented by the Prosecution, Mr. Registrar, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1053 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, can you close the bundle that's in front of you, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, we are still in private session. I should have turned into open session, although I asked for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That clearly -- judgement clearly should have been given in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. In open session, my first order will be to make public all that has been said since we resumed after the break. That will be public transcripts. The Chamber has put a question to Mr. Josse as to whether P780 was objected, and after that the Chamber delivered its decision on not allowing two documents to be shown to the witness and three documents to be marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You, Mr. Savkic, have produced for the Court two statements in 1991 relating to arms smuggling. After that time, that's middle-to-late 1991, did the illegal supply of arms cease in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it continued throughout all this period and later on, i.e., in 1991, many of these findings were reported to us Serbs who participated in subsequent negotiations but also to Muslims. And these are two statements that we have in front of us amongst others, one of them being this statement given by the imam.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, who reported to you that illegal arms were being supplied? Who did the reporting, in other words?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports were oral and given to us by the chief of the public security station from Vlasenica, but there were other sources as well through which some of us received the exact data as to how this armament was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to break that down. The chief of public security station in Vlasenica, can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. His name was Radomir Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he was someone you knew. Correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before he was appointed chief, he worked in the same company as I did. He was the head of the directorate for the development of the entire company.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll come back to him in one moment. Did you see with your own eyes illegal arms supply?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What then did Mr. Bjelanovic tell you about what was going on in this regard?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said a lot of things. He told us what the imam stated. Then he also told us about some previous ones. He also told us about the information that the Muslims were being armed on a large scale under the patronage of the highest MUP officials, and this line went from Hungary, via Croatia, Kladanj, all the way down to Sarajevo. He even mentioned that the person behind all that was the person who was in charge of the police in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was very soon after that replaced, but he remained in the position of an advisor to the minister of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. His name was Avdo Hebib.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am in the Chamber's hands. Am I allowed to ask the witness what the imam apparently said to the chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Josse, the Chamber does not allow you to ask the witness about what was said, in view of the not-resolved Rule 95 concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My only observation, of course, is the Defence are worse off having presented the document in the first place. Had we not presented the document in the first place, no objection could have been taken. The hearsay evidence would have been given and would have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would not have known if the Prosecution would have presented their concerns about what the basis was about their information of any statement given to a police officer by an imam in -- in Vlasenica. So we do not know, as a matter of fact, you're worse off or whether you're in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You are prevented, Mr. Savkic, for the avoidance of any doubt, of telling the Court what the imam said to the chief of the public security station. You're also prevented from telling the Court any information you learned from the person named in tab 8. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand I can't say this; however, all the citizens of Vlasenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's important that you acknowledge you understand that for the questions I'm now going to ask you. Did the chief of the public security station tell you of anyone else, other than the person named in tab 2 and in tab 8, who supplied information to him about the smuggling of arms?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were other individuals, particularly when it came to the armament of Muslims in the area of Bratunac municipality. There was an official line through the MUP when it came to this armament. There were some other things relative to Zepa, but mostly those were sources that spoke to him and provided him with all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of those sources of information?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to remember any names. In any case, the story would be the same. Those were either Serbs or Muslims who did not want their identity to be revealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of military or paramilitary activity, when did it become apparent to you, if at all, that the Muslims were armed in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally saw, when it comes to the uniformed paramilitaries who were later on identified as the Patriotic League. I personally saw them at the beginning of February and beginning of March -- the end of February and beginning of March 1992 as I was returning from a meeting where we from the Boksit company spoke to the inhabitants of Djilovici [phoen] a small place in the vicinity of the mine. As I was on my way back to Milici I was travelling in a Jeep. I was there together with the driver of Ibro Nuhanovic, and his name was Sretko Relic [phoen]. And there was another Muslim whose name I can't recall. In the place called Sedric, at the crossroads I noticed from the direction of a village called Basca, a red Lada vehicle was coming towards us. There were four uniformed persons sitting in it with green berets and metal round badge. Next to the driver there was an automatic rifle, and I also noticed that the person sitting in the back also had weapons. One had a semi-automatic rifle, and the other one was holding an automatic rifle in his lap. Although the badge was rather big, its diameter must have been two or two and a half centimetres, so I could see it well. And later on, in combat I noticed the symbol of crescent and the star, and I don't know what the inscription was on the badge. So, in other words, this was my first sighting of the paramilitary formation called the Patriotic League. Every year from the year 1996 onwards in September or in October in Tuzla there is a celebration of the anniversary of the foundation of the Patriotic League which took place in Tuzla in 1991. In this case, my first contact with this military formation of the Muslim people, the paramilitary formation, was when I have just said. And let me just add one more thing. Before that, in September or October, one of these extremists, Ibrahim Ademovic also known as Cakura, who resided in Mocila village, he stopped our buses and he chased our workers and forced them to return on foot. And he would appear with an automatic rifle M-56. Interestingly enough, the police had to intervene. The police was still mixed at the time in February and March 1993. He would capture them, he would ill-treat them, and he would do whatever he wanted to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And could that have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 3 would be D136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Looking at the B/C/S verse of this document, I suggest that everyone does, this is the back and front of some form of identity card. That's right, isn't it? Did you get my question, Mr. Savkic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you have the original of this with you in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do indeed. I have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not particularly anxious that it be surrendered as an exhibit, but the Court might wish to see it, Your Honour, because it's much clearer than that depicted in the photograph [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would just like to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you would just take that one document out of your bag, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We can see, Mr. Savkic, that this is a card indicating membership by this particular individual of the 16th Muslim Brigade, Bratunac Detachment. Were you aware in April of 1992, early April of 1992, that there was a 16th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please explain. Are you referring to the entire month of April or the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if at this stage we could object. It's not clear to us from the translation we have that the document before the Court and the witness establishes the proposition that's contained in my learned friend's question. So I don't think it's appropriate for him to lead on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll deal with it differently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look, if we may, at the card. We see -- you've got the photocopy of it in front of you, Mr. Savkic. We look at the bottom part. We see on the left-hand corner three words. The first one is -- begins S-l-u-z-b-a. Can you read those three words out, please. You're not sure what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's a date. We see a date at number 1, bottom part of the photocopy. What are the three words above the date. Read them out.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Service in war."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then what is the date that you read underneath that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is 05/04/1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So let's use that date, bearing in mind Mr. Margetts' objection. At that time, 5th of April, 1992, did you know there was a 16th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend hasn't established the existence of such a brigade, and we now ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the document on the right, top, says: "16th Muslimanska Brigada," which of course could be the title of a book or whatever else. Let's move on. To the extent Mr. Josse is leading in the respect, the Chamber whole-heartedly allows him to lead. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Savkic, is: Did you know that a 16th Muslim Brigade existed on the 5th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that that was its name; however, its members didn't hide from anybody, absolutely not. Across the road from the assembly point of this brigade -- actually, across the brook there are Serbian villages of Glusac and Bisina, and from those positions one could easily see members of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did you understand that such a unit had been created?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, although at this moment from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at least officially, it had been ordered that the mobilisation of the TO should be carried out. It transpires very clearly from this booklet that this would be later; however, it is very clear from this booklet that this is not the Territorial Defence but the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with a document that is recognisable as -- as a document associated with a war unit, a unit that is engaged in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As of the 5th of April, 1992, were you aware of any public pronouncement by any Bosnian politician that ethnically based brigades should be set up?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said here, I cannot remember. However, there were all sorts of threats from the leadership of the SDA and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those of us who lived there heard that and saw those outpours and those speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've given some evidence about arming on the Muslim side. Prior to April 1992, shall we say the 1st of April, 1992, how did the Serbs respond to what you understood the Muslims were doing?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, and I am saying "unfortunately" because of all that would happen later on, the representatives of our people in Bosnia and Herzegovina were saying at the time that despite the obvious threats and indications from the ground, that in keeping with the institution of the federal state, the JNA was the only armed force that was allowed to exist in the territory of the federal state. They were also saying that the Yugoslav People's Army would provide protection to the Serbian people and all sorts of similar things. They were of the opinion that we should abide by the constitution and the laws. That was their explanation. This did provide a certain degree of guarantee and safety to the Serbs in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, truth be told, what had happened in Croatia already demonstrated that those guarantees were very weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move on to a separate but related subject, and let's take a look at tab 5. I think we can deal with this relatively shortly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, can we perhaps ask a few questions on the background of the document. How did you obtain this document of which I have the original now in my hands, Mr. Savkic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received the original probably -- or rather most certainly from the citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who are the citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about -- actually, the villagers of Serbian ethnicity of these two villages, Glusac and Bisina, or maybe this document was provided to me during that period of time when the village guards had already been set up around the Serbian villages. And those village guards were composed exclusively of the local villagers. In one or another way, I received this document. I received so many such documents during that period of time, and this is just one of them. So I wouldn't really be able to tell you exactly the name of the person who brought this document to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the -- is the person depicted and whose name is given, do you know whether he is still alive or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 5, please. That's already got a number; it's P258. This is a protocol of an agreement between the representatives of the Serbian and Muslim people. If we turn to the last page we see that it was signed by six community leaders on each side, one of which, at number -- well, number 4, you were one of the Serbian representatives. In essence, the agreement provided the municipality should be divided into Serbian and Muslim sectors, and a portion of it should be separated all together to form a new Milici municipality under Serbian control on the basis the population there was [indiscernible] Serbian. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And defines, with some detail, the areas such as towns and villages, how they should be divided, as well as outstanding issues for a future possible settlement. Why was this protocol agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it happened because reality forced us to get together and to try to find a reasonable way out of that situation that was genuinely difficult. I would appreciate it if the gentleman presiding over this court would allow me to say in a few words what the situation was like in the moment we made this agreement. In that period, there were many columns of vehicles passing through Vlasenica and Milici. Some came from Central Bosnia and Sarajevo, and the vehicles carried both Serbs and Muslims. Sometimes these motorcades were several kilometres long, and all of them were going to Serbia. From all the other direction such as Bratunac and, to a lesser extent, Srebrenica, and from Muslim villages in the municipality of Vlasenica, convoys of Muslims were going towards Sarajevo and the central part of Bosnia. From Croatia JNA units were coming back. To put it briefly, it was complete chaos. We had some insight into the weaponry situation, the weapons in the possession of private citizens. But especially relevant to Vlasenica in particular was the order of the SDA. I can't say whether it originated in the Municipal Board of the SDA or from the headquarters, but the order stipulated that women and elderly should be evacuated from all villages, but especially from Vlasenica itself. It was at that time that we reached an agreement among the parties, and prior to that this board for inter-ethnic cooperation in Vlasenica was set-up. And we agreed to find some practical solutions for our everyday problems. That's why we got together. I believe we sat down to talk two times, once, the first time, we made a draft; and the second time we fine-tuned the agreement. This agreement in the latter part contains the very messages that were the main purpose, namely, we said that since nothing, absolutely nothing, was functioning on the state level in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we were looking for a way to observe the principle of proportionate ethnic representation, because we all felt better being represented by members of our own ethnicity. So although the idea was based on this ethnic division, expect for Vlasenica where we left open the possibility, since it was a township after all, we left open the possibility for Serbs to live in Muslim neighbourhoods and Muslims to live in Serb neighbourhoods, this could work except in Nova Kasaba where, for instance, ten families of Serbs left -- were left living in a Muslim neighbourhood, neighbourhoods that belonged, in terms of population, to Muslims, but since they had a particular geographic position, this population was given to choose which area to exercise their rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Chamber wonders whether the witness is reading something?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, the document. He's referring to the document at tab 5. That's what he's got in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Savkic, you have the protocol in front of you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I have the protocol in front of me, and I only wanted to explain in greater detail how earnestly this was prepared, what possibilities were given to the citizens. What is important is that all important facilities remained intact. There were no divisions of pharmacies, the cultural hall, the schools, or the police. Everything was regulated. We even said on page 7 that newly established municipalities would ensure unhindered passage to JNA units, but due to fear from paramilitary formations it was desirable to give prior notification to the competent authorities of municipalities. We also appealed to the citizens to return to -- their weapons to the closest JNA unit because it was a fact of life that they had weapons. So if we look at this agreement, you have the introductory part - and this is important for the Judges to hear - at the proposal of parliamentary parties, citizens, alliances, the board for inter-ethnic cooperation. Some persons who had never been members of any political party, the SDA or the SDS, were also involved. And if you look at the body of our presentation, they are represented. It's important. The people involved were people who enjoyed the greatest respect among the people, high school and university professors, directors of enterprises, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's been suggested to this Chamber, Mr. Savkic, that the Serbs forced this protocol upon the Muslims. What do you say to that proposition?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of them, except for number 1, who is a Muslim -- the best would be to ask them. I have to stress again that those talks proceeded in a very correct, very decent manner. And I told you a bit yesterday about how everybody was affected by the history and the fate of this region. For instance, person on number 5, Saracevic Sejfo, who was then president of the court, it would be a good idea to invite him so he can tell you, or person number 3, Saban Avdic, he used to be my teacher, the person under number 1 or number 3, director of the school in Vlasenica and professor of philosophy. Any one of them, Mihajlo Bajagic, a very moderate, quiet man, could be a good witness to that. They all know what we did; we did our job honourably. On the 14th of April, the Assembly in its full composition adopted this protocol without any modifications, and that is also recorded in an official document. I have to say that not all deputies were present, not all Muslim deputies were present, but out of those present a large number also voted in favour of this agreement. As to those who did not attend, I can tell you later why they didn't. In that period while we were looking for this agreed solution, they were busy setting up Crisis Staffs in Muslim enclaves and preparing for armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
